claim: ASARs are a family of very-long noncoding RNAs that control replication timing on individual human autosomes.
source: ASARs are a family of very-long noncoding RNAs that control replication timing on individual human autosomes, and are essential for chromosome stability.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a primary finding of the research.

claim: ASARs are essential for chromosome stability.
source: ASARs are a family of very-long noncoding RNAs that control replication timing on individual human autosomes, and are essential for chromosome stability.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a primary finding.

claim: The eight known ASAR lncRNAs remain closely associated with their parent chromosomes.
source: The eight known ASAR lncRNAs remain closely associated with their parent chromosomes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Analysis of RNA-protein interaction data from ENCODE revealed numerous RBPs with significant interactions with multiple ASAR lncRNAs.
source: Analysis of RNA-protein interaction data (from ENCODE) revealed numerous RBPs with significant interactions with multiple ASAR lncRNAs, with several hnRNPs as abundant interactors.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by eCLIP data analysis shown in the results.

claim: Several hnRNPs are abundant interactors with ASAR lncRNAs.
source: Analysis of RNA-protein interaction data (from ENCODE) revealed numerous RBPs with significant interactions with multiple ASAR lncRNAs, with several hnRNPs as abundant interactors.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by eCLIP data analysis.

claim: An ~7 kb domain within the ASAR6-141 lncRNA shows a striking density of RBP interaction sites.
source: An ~7 kb domain within the ASAR6-141 lncRNA shows a striking density of RBP interaction sites.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by eCLIP data in Figure 1.

claim: The ~7 kb RNA binding protein domain contains functional sequences for controlling replication timing of entire chromosomes in cis.
source: Genetic deletion and ectopic integration assays indicate that this ~7 kb RNA binding protein domain contains functional sequences for controlling replication timing of entire chromosomes in cis.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by deletion and transgene integration experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: shRNA-mediated depletion of HNRNPA1 results in dissociation of ASAR lncRNAs from their chromosome territories.
source: shRNA-mediated depletion of 10 different RNA binding proteins, including HNRNPA1, HNRNPC, HNRNPL, HNRNPM, HNRNPU, or HNRNPUL1, results in dissociation of ASAR lncRNAs from their chromosome territories, and disrupts the synchronous replication that occurs on all autosome pairs, recapitulating the effect of individual ASAR knockouts on a genome-wide scale.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by RNA-FISH experiments in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: shRNA-mediated depletion of HNRNPC results in dissociation of ASAR lncRNAs from their chromosome territories.
source: shRNA-mediated depletion of 10 different RNA binding proteins, including HNRNPA1, HNRNPC, HNRNPL, HNRNPM, HNRNPU, or HNRNPUL1, results in dissociation of ASAR lncRNAs from their chromosome territories, and disrupts the synchronous replication that occurs on all autosome pairs, recapitulating the effect of individual ASAR knockouts on a genome-wide scale.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by RNA-FISH experiments in Figures 3 and 5.

evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by RNA-FISH experiments in Figures 3 and 5.

source: shRNA-mediated depletion of 10 different RNA binding proteins, including HNRNPA1, HNRNPC, HNRNPL, HNRNPM, HNRNPU, or HNRNPUL1, results in dissociation of ASAR lncRNAs from their chromosome territories, and disrupts the synchronous replication that occurs on all autosome pairs, recapitulating the effect of individual ASAR knockouts on a genome-wide scale.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by RNA-FISH experiments in Figures 3 and 5.

source: shRNA-mediated depletion of 10 different RNA binding proteins, including HNRNPA1, HNRNPC, HNRNPL, HNRNPM, HNRNPU, or HNRNPUL1, results in dissociation of ASAR lncRNAs from their chromosome territories, and disrupts the synchronous replication that occurs on all autosome pairs, recapitulating the effect of individual ASAR knockouts on a genome-wide scale.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by RNA-FISH experiments in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: shRNA-mediated depletion of HNRNPUL1 results in dissociation of ASAR lncRNAs from their chromosome territories.
source: shRNA-mediated depletion of 10 different RNA binding proteins, including HNRNPA1, HNRNPC, HNRNPL, HNRNPM, HNRNPU, or HNRNPUL1, results in dissociation of ASAR lncRNAs from their chromosome territories, and disrupts the synchronous replication that occurs on all autosome pairs, recapitulating the effect of individual ASAR knockouts on a genome-wide scale.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by RNA-FISH experiments in Figures 3 and 5.

claim: shRNA-mediated depletion of specific RBPs disrupts the synchronous replication that occurs on all autosome pairs.
source: shRNA-mediated depletion of 10 different RNA binding proteins, including HNRNPA1, HNRNPC, HNRNPL, HNRNPM, HNRNPU, or HNRNPUL1, results in dissociation of ASAR lncRNAs from their chromosome territories, and disrupts the synchronous replication that occurs on all autosome pairs, recapitulating the effect of individual ASAR knockouts on a genome-wide scale.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and demonstrated by BrdU replication timing assays in Figure 6.

claim: RBP depletion recapitulates the effect of individual ASAR knockouts on a genome-wide scale.
source: shRNA-mediated depletion of 10 different RNA binding proteins, including HNRNPA1, HNRNPC, HNRNPL, HNRNPM, HNRNPU, or HNRNPUL1, results in dissociation of ASAR lncRNAs from their chromosome territories, and disrupts the synchronous replication that occurs on all autosome pairs, recapitulating the effect of individual ASAR knockouts on a genome-wide scale.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by comparison of RBP depletion phenotypes with ASAR knockout phenotypes.

claim: ASARs function as essential RNA scaffolds for the assembly of hnRNP complexes that help maintain the structural integrity of each mammalian chromosome.
source: Our results further demonstrate the role that ASARs play during the temporal order of genome-wide replication, and we propose that ASARs function as essential RNA scaffolds for the assembly of hnRNP complexes that help maintain the structural integrity of each mammalian chromosome.
evidence: This is proposed in the abstract based on the experimental findings.

claim: The vast majority of mammalian DNA replicates in homologous regions of chromosome pairs in a highly synchronous manner.
source: The vast majority of mammalian DNA replicates in homologous regions of chromosome pairs in a highly synchronous manner (Mukhopadhyay et al., 2014; Dileep and Gilbert, 2018; Rivera-Mulia et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Genetic disruption of ASAR loci causes a delay in replication timing on individual human chromosomes in cis.
source: However, genetic disruption of non-protein coding ASAR ('ASynchronous replication and Autosomal RNA') loci causes a delay in replication timing on individual human chromosomes in cis, resulting in highly asynchronous replication between pairs of autosomes (Donley et al., 2015; Heskett et al., 2020; Heskett et al., 2022; Stoffregen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations to previous work.

claim: Genetic disruption of ASAR loci results in highly asynchronous replication between pairs of autosomes.
source: However, genetic disruption of non-protein coding ASAR ('ASynchronous replication and Autosomal RNA') loci causes a delay in replication timing on individual human chromosomes in cis, resulting in highly asynchronous replication between pairs of autosomes (Donley et al., 2015; Heskett et al., 2020; Heskett et al., 2022; Stoffregen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: There are eight genetically validated ASARs located on human chromosomes 1, 6, 8, 9, and 15.
source: There are eight genetically validated ASARs that are located on human chromosomes 1, 6, 8, 9, and 15 (Donley et al., 2015; Heskett et al., 2020; Heskett et al., 2022; Stoffregen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: All known ASAR lncRNAs have contiguously transcribed regions of >180 kb.
source: All of the known ASAR lncRNAs share several distinctive characteristics, including: (1) contiguously transcribed regions of >180 kb, (2) epigenetically regulated allelic expression imbalance (AEI; including mono-allelic expression); (3) variable epigenetic replication timing (VERT; including asynchronous replication timing); (4) high density of LINE1 (L1) sequences (>30%); and (5) retention of the RNA within their parent chromosome territory.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a characteristic of ASARs.

claim: All known ASAR lncRNAs show epigenetically regulated allelic expression imbalance.
source: All of the known ASAR lncRNAs share several distinctive characteristics, including: (1) contiguously transcribed regions of >180 kb, (2) epigenetically regulated allelic expression imbalance (AEI; including mono-allelic expression); (3) variable epigenetic replication timing (VERT; including asynchronous replication timing); (4) high density of LINE1 (L1) sequences (>30%); and (5) retention of the RNA within their parent chromosome territory.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a characteristic of ASARs.

claim: All known ASAR lncRNAs show variable epigenetic replication timing.
source: All of the known ASAR lncRNAs share several distinctive characteristics, including: (1) contiguously transcribed regions of >180 kb, (2) epigenetically regulated allelic expression imbalance (AEI; including mono-allelic expression); (3) variable epigenetic replication timing (VERT; including asynchronous replication timing); (4) high density of LINE1 (L1) sequences (>30%); and (5) retention of the RNA within their parent chromosome territory.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a characteristic of ASARs.

claim: All known ASAR lncRNAs have high density of LINE1 sequences (>30%).
source: All of the known ASAR lncRNAs share several distinctive characteristics, including: (1) contiguously transcribed regions of >180 kb, (2) epigenetically regulated allelic expression imbalance (AEI; including mono-allelic expression); (3) variable epigenetic replication timing (VERT; including asynchronous replication timing); (4) high density of LINE1 (L1) sequences (>30%); and (5) retention of the RNA within their parent chromosome territory.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a characteristic of ASARs.

claim: All known ASAR lncRNAs show retention of the RNA within their parent chromosome territory.
source: All of the known ASAR lncRNAs share several distinctive characteristics, including: (1) contiguously transcribed regions of >180 kb, (2) epigenetically regulated allelic expression imbalance (AEI; including mono-allelic expression); (3) variable epigenetic replication timing (VERT; including asynchronous replication timing); (4) high density of LINE1 (L1) sequences (>30%); and (5) retention of the RNA within their parent chromosome territory.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a characteristic of ASARs.

claim: 68 ASAR candidates have been identified on every human autosome.
source: Recently, we used these notable characteristics to identify 68 ASAR candidates on every human autosome (Heskett et al., 2020; Heskett et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: ASAR6 lncRNA expressed from transgenes remains associated with the chromosome territories where they are transcribed.
source: For example, ASAR6 lncRNA expressed from transgenes, ranging in size from an ~180 kb BAC transgene to PCR products (as small as ~3 kb) containing the critical sequences, remain associated with the chromosome territories where they are transcribed (Donley et al., 2013; Platt et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: ASAR6 transgenes cause delayed replication timing of entire chromosomes in cis.
source: These same transgenes cause delayed replication timing (DRT) and delayed mitotic condensation (DMC) of entire chromosomes in cis (Donley et al., 2013; Platt et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: ASAR6 transgenes cause delayed mitotic condensation of entire chromosomes in cis.
source: These same transgenes cause delayed replication timing (DRT) and delayed mitotic condensation (DMC) of entire chromosomes in cis (Donley et al., 2013; Platt et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: ASAR6 lncRNA controls chromosome-wide replication timing.
source: Furthermore, ASAR6 lncRNA was found to control chromosome-wide replication timing using oligonucleotide-mediated RNA degradation of ASAR6 lncRNA that was expressed from a BAC transgene integrated into mouse chromosome 3 (Platt et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: ASARs represent ubiquitous, essential, cis-acting elements that control mammalian chromosome replication timing via expression of chromosome associated RNAs.
source: These findings suggest that ASARs represent ubiquitous, essential, cis-acting elements that control mammalian chromosome replication timing via expression of chromosome associated RNAs.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an interpretation of previous findings.

claim: Chromosome-associated long non-coding RNAs are important for numerous aspects of chromosome dynamics in diverse eukaryotes from yeast to mammals.
source: Chromosome-associated long non-coding RNAs are known to be important for numerous aspects of chromosome dynamics in diverse eukaryotes from yeast to mammals (Ding et al., 2019; Faber and Vo, 2022; Nozawa and Gilbert, 2019; Creamer et al., 2021; Menon and Meller, 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The mammalian nucleus is rich in heterogenous nuclear RNA (hnRNA), which represents >95% of the total RNA Polymerase II output.
source: The mammalian nucleus is rich in heterogenous nuclear RNA (hnRNA), which represents >95% of the total RNA Polymerase II output (Nozawa and Gilbert, 2019; St Laurent et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Long nascent transcripts detected by C0T-1 DNA play a dynamic structural role that promotes the open architecture of active chromosome territories.
source: Previous studies have suggested that long nascent transcripts that are detected by C0T-1 DNA play a dynamic structural role that promotes the open architecture of active chromosome territories (Creamer et al., 2021; Hall et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: RNA species detected by C0T-1 DNA are predominantly L1 sequences.
source: The RNA species detected by C0T-1 DNA are predominantly L1 sequences, and these L1 RNAs remain associated with the chromosome territories where they are transcribed (Hall et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: L1 RNAs remain associated with the chromosome territories where they are transcribed.
source: The RNA species detected by C0T-1 DNA are predominantly L1 sequences, and these L1 RNAs remain associated with the chromosome territories where they are transcribed (Hall et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The critical sequences for controlling chromosome-wide replication timing within ASAR6 and ASAR15 map to the antisense strand of L1 sequences.
source: In addition, deletion and ectopic integration assays demonstrated that the critical sequences for controlling chromosome-wide replication timing within ASAR6 and ASAR15 map to the antisense strand of L1 sequences located within the ASAR6 and ASAR15 lncRNAs (Platt et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Human C0T-1 DNA can detect the chromosome territory localization of ASAR6 lncRNA expressed from a BAC transgene integrated into a mouse chromosome.
source: In this report we found that human C0T-1 DNA can detect the chromosome territory localization of ASAR6 lncRNA that is expressed from a BAC transgene integrated into a mouse chromosome, indicating that at least some of the RNA species detected by C0T-1 DNA represents ASAR lncRNA.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and demonstrated in Figure 7.

claim: At least some of the RNA species detected by C0T-1 DNA represents ASAR lncRNA.
source: In this report we found that human C0T-1 DNA can detect the chromosome territory localization of ASAR6 lncRNA that is expressed from a BAC transgene integrated into a mouse chromosome, indicating that at least some of the RNA species detected by C0T-1 DNA represents ASAR lncRNA.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and demonstrated in Figure 7.

claim: Heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoproteins (hnRNPs) represent a large family of abundant RBPs that contribute to multiple aspects of nucleic acid metabolism.
source: Heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoproteins (hnRNPs) represent a large family of abundant RBPs that contribute to multiple aspects of nucleic acid metabolism.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as background knowledge.

claim: Most hnRNPs possess conventional nuclear localization signals and are predominantly present in the nucleus during steady state.
source: Most of the hnRNPs possess conventional nuclear localization signals and are predominantly present in the nucleus during steady state, where they function in various RNA metabolic processes including transcription, splicing, nuclear export, and 3' end processing (Geuens et al., 2016; Domanski et al., 2022), and more recently have been implicated in DNA replication (Connolly et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: hnRNPs function in various RNA metabolic processes including transcription, splicing, nuclear export, and 3' end processing.
source: Most of the hnRNPs possess conventional nuclear localization signals and are predominantly present in the nucleus during steady state, where they function in various RNA metabolic processes including transcription, splicing, nuclear export, and 3' end processing (Geuens et al., 2016; Domanski et al., 2022), and more recently have been implicated in DNA replication (Connolly et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: hnRNPs have been implicated in DNA replication.
source: Most of the hnRNPs possess conventional nuclear localization signals and are predominantly present in the nucleus during steady state, where they function in various RNA metabolic processes including transcription, splicing, nuclear export, and 3' end processing (Geuens et al., 2016; Domanski et al., 2022), and more recently have been implicated in DNA replication (Connolly et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: siRNA mediated depletion of HNRNPU results in dissociation of C0T-1 RNA from chromosome territories.
source: A direct connection between chromosome territory associated C0T-1 RNA and hnRNPs was established by the observation that siRNA mediated depletion, or forced expression of dominant interfering mutants, of HNRNPU results in dissociation of C0T-1 RNA from chromosome territories (Creamer et al., 2021; Hall et al., 2014; Kolpa et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Forced expression of dominant interfering mutants of HNRNPU results in dissociation of C0T-1 RNA from chromosome territories.
source: A direct connection between chromosome territory associated C0T-1 RNA and hnRNPs was established by the observation that siRNA mediated depletion, or forced expression of dominant interfering mutants, of HNRNPU results in dissociation of C0T-1 RNA from chromosome territories (Creamer et al., 2021; Hall et al., 2014; Kolpa et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: HNRNPU nonspecifically interacts with 'RNA debris' that creates a dynamic nuclear mesh that regulates interphase chromatin structure.
source: In addition, recent studies have proposed that abundant nuclear proteins such as HNRNPU nonspecifically interact with 'RNA debris' that creates a dynamic nuclear mesh that regulates interphase chromatin structure (Nozawa and Gilbert, 2019; Nozawa et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: ASAR6-141 lncRNA is localized within one of the chromosome 6 territories in male HTD114 cells.
source: Examples of mono-allelic expression and chromosome territory localization of ASAR6-141 lncRNA are shown in Figure 1A and B, where ASAR6-141 lncRNA is localized within one of the chromosome 6 territories in two different cell types, male HTD114 cells and female GM12878 cells, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: ASAR6-141 lncRNA is localized within one of the chromosome 6 territories in female GM12878 cells.
source: Examples of mono-allelic expression and chromosome territory localization of ASAR6-141 lncRNA are shown in Figure 1A and B, where ASAR6-141 lncRNA is localized within one of the chromosome 6 territories in two different cell types, male HTD114 cells and female GM12878 cells, respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The size of RNA hybridization signals detected by ASAR probes are variable.
source: We note that the size of the RNA hybridization signals detected by all ASAR probes are variable, ranging in size from large clouds that occupy entire chromosome territories, with similarity in appearance to XIST RNA 'clouds' (Figure 1B), to relatively small sites of hybridization that remain tightly associated with the expressed alleles (Donley et al., 2015; Heskett et al., 2020; Heskett et al., 2022; Stoffregen et al., 2011) .
evidence: This is stated in the results with supporting citations and reference to Figure 1B.

claim: 99 different RBPs have significant binding peaks that map within four ASAR lncRNAs.
source: Utilizing the eCLIP peaks previously identified by ENCODE (Moore et al., 2020) we found significant RBP binding peaks for 99 different RBPs that map within the four ASAR lncRNAs (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results based on analysis of eCLIP data.

claim: ASAR6-141 displays significant RBP interactions for 35 different RBPs across the transcribed region.
source: An example of this analysis is shown in Figure 1C, where ASAR6-141 displays significant RBP interactions for 35 different RBPs across the transcribed region.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: An ~7 kb region within ASAR6-141 contained virtually all of the significant eCLIP peaks in both K562 and HepG2 cell lines.
source: Given the contiguous expression (RNAseq from total RNA) across the ~185 kb ASAR6-141 locus in both K562 and HepG2 cell lines (Figure 1G) and the abundant eCLIP reads from 35 different RBPs in 10 kb windows across the ASAR6-141 lncRNA (Figure 1C and D; see Figure 1—source data 2), we were surprised to detect an ~7 kb region that contained virtually all of the significant eCLIP peaks in both cell lines (Figure 1G; and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1G.

claim: 58 independent eCLIP peaks of RBP interactions are within the ~7 kb RNA binding protein domain.
source: The zoomed in view in Figure 1G shows alignment of 58 independent eCLIP peaks of RBP interactions within the ~7 kb RNA binding protein domain (RBPD).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Deletion of the ~7 kb RBPD from the expressed allele resulted in a significant delay in replication timing.
source: Quantification of the BrdU incorporation in CHR6B and CHR6A in multiple cells indicated that deletion of the ~7 kb RBPD from the expressed allele resulted in a significant delay in replication timing (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Deletion of the ~7 kb RBPD from the silent allele does not result in delayed replication timing.
source: This is in contrast to cells prior to deletion, or in cells containing a deletion of the ~7 kb RBPD from the silent allele (CHR6A), where the BrdU incorporation is comparable between CHR6A and CHR6B (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Homozygous deletions of the 7 kb RBPD show an asynchronous replication pattern.
source: In addition, an asynchronous replication pattern was also present in cells with homozygous deletions of the 7 kb RBPD, with CHR6B representing the later replicating allele (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The delayed replication associated with deletion of the ~7 kb RBPD on CHR6B is comparable to the delayed replication associated with deletion of the entire ASAR6-141 locus from the same chromosome.
source: Furthermore, we found that the delayed replication associated with deletion of the ~7 kb RBPD on CHR6B is comparable to the delayed replication associated with deletion of the entire ASAR6-141 locus from the same chromosome (i.e. CHR6B; Figure 2E; also see Heskett et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2E with reference to previous work.

claim: The ~7 kb RBPD contains functional sequences for controlling replication timing.
source: These results indicate that the ~7 kb RBPD contains functional sequences for controlling replication timing, and further supports the conclusion that the expressed allele but not the silent allele controls replication timing of human chromosome 6 (Heskett et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the results as an interpretation of the deletion experiments.

claim: The expressed allele but not the silent allele controls replication timing of human chromosome 6.
source: These results indicate that the ~7 kb RBPD contains functional sequences for controlling replication timing, and further supports the conclusion that the expressed allele but not the silent allele controls replication timing of human chromosome 6 (Heskett et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the results with a supporting citation.

claim: Large clouds of RNA FISH hybridization signals comparable to Xist RNA were detected in 4 out of 12 clones expressing the sense transgene.
source: Large clouds of RNA FISH hybridization signals that are comparable to Xist RNA hybridization signals were detected in 4 out of 12 clones expressing the sense transgene (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2G.

claim: 0 out of 12 clones containing the antisense transgene expressed RNA FISH hybridization signals comparable to Xist RNA signals.
source: In contrast, 0 out of 12 clones containing the antisense transgene expressed RNA FISH hybridization signals comparable to Xist RNA signals, but instead only small pinpoint sites of RNA FISH hybridization were detected (Figure 2H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The ~7 kb RBPD RNA is localized within one of the chromosome 5 DNA hybridization signals.
source: Figure 2J shows that the ~7 kb RBPD RNA is localized within one of the chromosome 5 DNA hybridization signals, indicating that the ~7 kb RBPD RNA is retained within the chromosome 5 territory.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2J.

claim: The ~7 kb RBPD RNA is retained within the chromosome 5 territory.
source: Figure 2J shows that the ~7 kb RBPD RNA is localized within one of the chromosome 5 DNA hybridization signals, indicating that the ~7 kb RBPD RNA is retained within the chromosome 5 territory.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2J.

claim: The chromosome containing the ~7 kb RBPD sense strand transgene is delayed in mitotic condensation and contains more BrdU incorporation than any other chromosome within the same cell.
source: Figure 2K shows an example of this replication-timing assay in a mitotic cell containing the ~7 kb RBPD sense strand transgene integrated into mouse chromosome 5. Note that the chromosome containing the ~7 kb RBPD transgene is delayed in mitotic condensation and contains more BrdU incorporation than any other chromosome within the same cell.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2K.

claim: Integration of the transgene with the ~7 kb RBPD in the antisense orientation did not result in delayed condensation nor in delayed replication of mouse chromosomes.
source: In contrast, integration of the transgene with the ~7 kb RBPD in the antisense orientation did not result in delayed condensation nor in delayed replication of mouse chromosomes (Figure 2L).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2L.

claim: shRNA depletion of HNRNPU results in a significant depletion of the protein.
source: Quantitation of the immunofluorescence for each RBP in empty vector versus shRNA expressing cells, indicated a significant depletion of each RBP (Figure 3K; also see Figure 3—figure supplement 1 for western blots).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3K and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Cells expressing shRNAs directed at HNRNPU showed a nearly complete absence of the highly localized nuclear RNA hybridization signals for ASAR6-141 lncRNA.
source: In contrast, cells expressing shRNAs directed at HNRNPU, HNRNPUL1, HNRNPC, HNRNPM, HLTF, HNRNPA1, HNRNPL, KHSRP, or UCHL5 showed a nearly complete absence of the highly localized nuclear RNA hybridization signals for ASAR6-141 lncRNA, and the appearance of large punctate cytoplasmic hybridization signals (Figure 3M–U).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3M-U.

claim: Cells expressing shRNAs directed at HNRNPU showed the appearance of large punctate cytoplasmic hybridization signals for ASAR6-141 lncRNA.
source: In contrast, cells expressing shRNAs directed at HNRNPU, HNRNPUL1, HNRNPC, HNRNPM, HLTF, HNRNPA1, HNRNPL, KHSRP, or UCHL5 showed a nearly complete absence of the highly localized nuclear RNA hybridization signals for ASAR6-141 lncRNA, and the appearance of large punctate cytoplasmic hybridization signals (Figure 3M–U).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3M-U.

claim: Cells expressing shRNAs directed at PTBP1 showed only the typical nuclear localized hybridization signals for both ASAR6-141 and XIST lncRNAs.
source: In contrast, cells expressing shRNAs directed at PTBP1, PTBP2, or MATR3 showed only the typical nuclear localized hybridization signals for both ASAR6-141 and XIST lncRNAs (Figure 3V; and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3V and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Localized nuclear XIST RNA hybridization signals were detected in all shRNA treated cells.
source: In addition, localized nuclear XIST RNA hybridization signals were detected in all shRNA treated cells (Figure 3M–V and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3M-V and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cytoplasmic foci of XIST RNA hybridization colocalized with ASAR6-141 lncRNA were detected following RBP depletion.
source: However, we detected cytoplasmic foci of XIST RNA hybridization that colocalized with the ASAR6-141 lncRNA, and a significant decrease in the size of the nuclear XIST RNA hybridization signals (Figure 3W).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3W.

claim: A significant decrease in the size of the nuclear XIST RNA hybridization signals was detected following RBP depletion.
source: However, we detected cytoplasmic foci of XIST RNA hybridization that colocalized with the ASAR6-141 lncRNA, and a significant decrease in the size of the nuclear XIST RNA hybridization signals (Figure 3W).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3W.

claim: At least some of the XIST RNA was dissociated from the inactive X chromosome and colocalized with ASAR6-141 lncRNA in large cytoplasmic foci.
source: These observations indicate that at least some of the XIST RNA was dissociated from the inactive X chromosome and colocalized with ASAR6-141 lncRNA in large cytoplasmic foci.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an interpretation of the RNA-FISH data.

claim: The intensity of the Xist RNA FISH signal was enhanced in the region where the ~7 kb RBPD hybridization signal was detected.
source: We note that the intensity of the Xist RNA FISH signal was enhanced in the region where the ~7 kb RBPD hybridization signal was detected (Figure 4B), suggesting that the presence of the ~7 kb RBPD RNA promoted preferential localization of Xist RNA in the same region of the X chromosome territory that contains the ~7 kb RBPD RNA.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The presence of the ~7 kb RBPD RNA promoted preferential localization of Xist RNA in the same region of the X chromosome territory that contains the ~7 kb RBPD RNA.
source: We note that the intensity of the Xist RNA FISH signal was enhanced in the region where the ~7 kb RBPD hybridization signal was detected (Figure 4B), suggesting that the presence of the ~7 kb RBPD RNA promoted preferential localization of Xist RNA in the same region of the X chromosome territory that contains the ~7 kb RBPD RNA.
evidence: This is stated in the results as an interpretation of the RNA-FISH data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: X chromosomes with DMC contain the ~7 kb RBPD transgene.
source: During this analysis, we detected DMC on X chromosomes, and the X chromosomes with DMC contain the ~7 kb RBPD transgene (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: Integration of the 7 kb RBPD transgene is sufficient to cause DRT/DMC on the inactive X chromosome.
source: We conclude that integration of the 7 kb RBPD transgene is sufficient to cause DRT/DMC on the inactive X chromosome.
evidence: This is stated in the results as a conclusion from the transgene integration experiments.

claim: Cells with shRNA depletion of HNRNPA1 showed a dispersed punctate nuclear pattern for both ASAR1-187 and ASAR6 RNAs.
source: In contrast, cells with shRNA depletion of HNRNPA1, HNRNPC, HNRNPL, HNRNPM, HNRNPU, HLTF, KHSRP, or UCHL5 showed a dispersed punctate nuclear pattern for both ASAR RNAs (Figure 5D–K).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5D-K.

claim: Large punctate cytoplasmic foci were detected following RBP depletion, with the two ASAR RNA hybridization signals colocalized.
source: In addition, large punctate cytoplasmic foci were detected, with the two ASAR RNA hybridization signals colocalized.
evidence: This is stated in the results describing the RNA-FISH patterns after RBP depletion.

claim: Cells expressing shRNA against HNRNPU show loss of the chromosome associated RNA hybridization signals for both ASAR1-187 and ASAR6 RNAs.
source: In contrast, cells expressing shRNA against HNRNPU show loss of the chromosome associated RNA hybridization signals for both ASAR RNAs, and instead show diffuse nuclear and cytoplasmic hybridization, with the presence of large punctate cytoplasmic foci that hybridize to both ASAR RNA FISH probes (Figure 5O–Q).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5O-Q.

claim: Expression of shRNAs against SAFB, SAFB2, SAFB plus SAFB2, CTCF, or MATR3 did not alter the ASAR1-187 or ASAR6 RNA nuclear hybridization signals in HTD114 cells.
source: In contrast, expression of shRNAs against SAFB, SAFB2, SAFB plus SAFB2, CTCF, or MATR3 did not alter the ASAR1-187 or ASAR6 RNA nuclear hybridization signals in HTD114 cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 2E–J).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2E-J.

claim: Each autosome pair displays a stereotypical and synchronous BrdU incorporation pattern in cells expressing empty vector.
source: Using the BrdU terminal label assay (Smith et al., 2001; Smith and Thayer, 2012) in cells expressing the empty vector, we found that each autosome pair displays a stereotypical and synchronous BrdU incorporation pattern (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Following HNRNPU depletion, individual mitotic spreads displayed dramatic differential incorporation of BrdU into pairs of homologous chromosomes.
source: In contrast, following HNRNPU depletion, individual mitotic spreads displayed dramatic differential incorporation of BrdU into pairs of homologous chromosomes, examples of asynchronous replication timing between every pair of autosomes are shown in Figure 6B.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Chromosomes 1 and 6 display significant asynchrony following depletion of HNRNPU, HNRNPUL1, HLTF, KHSRP, UCHL5, or HNRNPA1.
source: Quantification of the BrdU incorporation in chromosomes 1 and 6 (see Figure 6—figure supplement 1) in multiple cells depleted for HNRNPU, HNRNPUL1, HLTF, KHSRP, UCHL5, or HNRNPA1 indicated that both pairs of chromosomes display significant asynchrony (Figure 6E and F).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6E and F.

claim: The DRT/DMC phenotype was detected in ~30% of mitotic spreads following shRNA-mediated depletions.
source: In addition, the DRT/DMC phenotype was detected in ~30% of mitotic spreads following shRNA-mediated depletions (two examples are shown in Figure 6G and H; also see Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6G, H, and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: shRNA-mediated depletion of HNRNPC, HNRNPL and HNRNPM resulted in dramatic alterations in chromosome morphology that included asynchronous replication and abnormal mitotic condensation.
source: Furthermore, shRNA-mediated depletion of HNRNPC, HNRNPL and HNRNPM resulted in dramatic alterations in chromosome morphology that included asynchronous replication and abnormal mitotic condensation, including ~10% of mitotic spreads with one or more chromosomes that displayed the DRT/DMC phenotype (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: C0T-1 DNA can detect ASAR6 RNA expressed from a BAC transgene integrated into mouse chromosome 3.
source: Because human C0T-1 DNA does not cross hybridize with mouse RNA or DNA in FISH assays (Hall et al., 2014), we were able to detect the chromosome territory localized expression of human ASAR6 RNA expressed from the transgene that is integrated into one of the mouse chromosome 3 homologs using human C0T-1 DNA as RNA FISH probe (Figure 7A and B), indicating that C0T-1 DNA detects ASAR6 RNA.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 7A and B.

claim: 68 ASAR candidates have been identified, and five out of five were genetically validated as controlling replication timing of individual human autosomes.
source: We recently identified 68 ASAR candidates, and genetically validated five out of five as controlling replication timing of individual human autosomes, bringing the total of genetically validated ASARs to eight (Donley et al., 2015; Heskett et al., 2020; Heskett et al., 2022; Stoffregen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: The total of genetically validated ASARs is eight.
source: We recently identified 68 ASAR candidates, and genetically validated five out of five as controlling replication timing of individual human autosomes, bringing the total of genetically validated ASARs to eight (Donley et al., 2015; Heskett et al., 2020; Heskett et al., 2022; Stoffregen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: An ~7 kb domain within the ~185 kb ASAR6-141 lncRNA contained virtually all of the significant peaks of RBP interactions in two different cell lines.
source: One unanticipated observation that came from this analysis was that an ~7 kb domain within the ~185 kb ASAR6-141 lncRNA contained virtually all of the significant peaks of RBP interactions in two different cell lines.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion summarizing the findings.

claim: Depletion of HNRNPA1, HNRNPC, HNRNPL, HNRNPM, HNRNPU, HNRNPUL1, HLTF, KHSRP, or UCHL5 dramatically altered the normally synchronous replication timing program of all autosome pairs.
source: We found that shRNA mediated depletion of 9 different ASAR-associated RBPs (HNRNPA1, HNRNPC, HNRNPL, HNRNPM, HNRNPU, HNRNPUL1, HLTF, KHSRP, or UCHL5) dramatically altered the normally synchronous replication timing program of all autosome pairs, recapitulating the effect of individual ASAR knockouts on a genome-wide scale.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion summarizing the findings.

claim: ASAR lncRNAs serve as essential RNA scaffolds for the assembly of multiple hnRNP/RBP complexes that function to maintain the structural integrity of each mammalian chromosome.
source: These results demonstrate the role that ASARs play during the temporal order of genome-wide replication, and suggests that ASAR lncRNAs serve as essential RNA scaffolds for the assembly of multiple hnRNP/RBP complexes that function to maintain the structural integrity of each mammalian chromosome.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: ASAR RNAs represent functional 'chromosome associated RNA' species that control chromosome dynamics within mammalian nuclei.
source: Given our recent discovery of ASAR RNAs expressed from every autosome, and encoded by ~3% of the human genome (Heskett et al., 2022), we propose that ASAR RNAs represent functional 'chromosome associated RNA' species that control chromosome dynamics within mammalian nuclei.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a proposal based on the findings.

claim: ASAR RNAs are encoded by ~3% of the human genome.
source: Given our recent discovery of ASAR RNAs expressed from every autosome, and encoded by ~3% of the human genome (Heskett et al., 2022), we propose that ASAR RNAs represent functional 'chromosome associated RNA' species that control chromosome dynamics within mammalian nuclei.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Several hnRNPs (HNRNPA1, HNRNPC, HNRNPL, HNRNPM, HNRNPU, and HNRNPUL1) are important interaction partners for the chromosome territory localization of multiple ASAR RNAs.
source: Here we identified several hnRNPs (HNRNPA1, HNRNPC, HNRNPL, HNRNPM, HNRNPU, and HNRNPUL1) as important interaction partners for the chromosome territory localization of multiple ASAR RNAs.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion summarizing the findings.

claim: HLTF is required for the chromosome territory localization of multiple ASAR RNAs and for the synchronous replication of every autosome pair.
source: In addition, we found that the SWI/SNF related transcription factor HLTF, which was recently shown to regulate replication fork reversal, prevent alternative mechanisms of stress-resistant DNA replication, and mediates cellular resistance to replication stress (Bai et al., 2020,) is required for the chromosome territory localization of multiple ASAR RNAs and for the synchronous replication of every autosome pair.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: KHSRP contributes to the chromosome territory localization of ASAR RNAs.
source: Furthermore, we found that the KH domain (HNRNPK Homology domain) containing protein KHSRP, and the ubiquitin hydrolase UCHL5 also contribute to the chromosome territory localization of ASAR RNAs.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion summarizing the findings.

claim: UCHL5 contributes to the chromosome territory localization of ASAR RNAs.
source: Furthermore, we found that the KH domain (HNRNPK Homology domain) containing protein KHSRP, and the ubiquitin hydrolase UCHL5 also contribute to the chromosome territory localization of ASAR RNAs.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion summarizing the findings.

claim: The association of ASAR RNAs with multiple hnRNPs in combination with other nuclear RBPs is an essential step in the regulation of the synchronous replication timing program on mammalian chromosomes.
source: Taken together our results indicate that the association of ASAR RNAs with multiple hnRNPs in combination with other nuclear RBPs is an essential step in the regulation of the synchronous replication timing program on mammalian chromosomes.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the findings.

claim: The RBP knockdowns that disrupt genome-wide synchronous replication also disrupt chromosome association of multiple ASAR RNAs.
source: However, the RBP knockdowns that disrupt genome-wide synchronous replication also disrupt chromosome association of multiple ASAR RNAs.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion summarizing the findings.

claim: The ability of an ectopically integrated ASAR6 transgene to cause delayed replication timing of a mouse chromosome required the ASAR6 RNA.
source: Our previous work demonstrated that the ability of an ectopically integrated ASAR6 transgene to cause delayed replication timing of a mouse chromosome required the ASAR6 RNA (Platt et al., 2018.)
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Displacement of ASAR RNA from chromosome territories upon RBP knockdown is a primary cause of the genome-wide replication timing asynchrony.
source: Hence, we expect that displacement of ASAR RNA from chromosome territories upon RBP knockdown is a primary cause of the genome-wide replication timing asynchrony, regardless of whether the displacement of ASAR RNA from the chromosome is a direct or indirect effect of RBP knockdown.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: HNRNPA1 and HNRNPC are components of the 40 S hnRNP particle, which forms a nuclear biomolecular condensate.
source: In support of this notion, HNRNPA1 and HNRNPC are components of the 40 S hnRNP particle, which forms a nuclear biomolecular condensate (Domanski et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: HNRNPU and HNRNPUL1 interact with each of the 40 S hnRNP particle subunits.
source: In addition, HNRNPU and HNRNPUL1 interact with each of the 40 S hnRNP particle subunits (Britton et al., 2014), suggesting the possibility of extensive protein-protein interactions.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: ASAR RNAs normally remain associated exclusively with the chromosome territory from which they are transcribed.
source: ASAR RNAs normally remain associated exclusively with the chromosome territory from which they are transcribed, and ASAR RNAs on different chromosomes remain separate.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion summarizing the normal behavior of ASAR RNAs.

claim: ASAR RNAs on different chromosomes remain separate.
source: ASAR RNAs normally remain associated exclusively with the chromosome territory from which they are transcribed, and ASAR RNAs on different chromosomes remain separate.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion summarizing the normal behavior of ASAR RNAs.

claim: RBP knockdowns that disrupt synchronous replication timing release ASAR RNAs from their chromosome territories, allowing colocalization of ASAR RNAs from different chromosomes.
source: RBP knockdowns that disrupt synchronous replication timing also release ASAR RNAs from their chromosome territories, allowing colocalization of ASAR RNAs from different chromosomes (i.e. ASAR6 and ASAR1-187, see Figure 5O–Q), often in nuclear and/or cytoplasmic foci reminiscent of the mixing of liquid-liquid phases.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in Figure 5O-Q.

claim: Xist RNA participates in the assembly of a nuclear heteromeric condensate essential for gene silencing on the inactive X chromosome.
source: Additional support for this model is the observation that Xist RNA participates in the assembly of a nuclear heteromeric condensate essential for gene silencing on the inactive X chromosome (Pandya-Jones et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

source: It is worth noting that ectopic integration of Xist transgenes has been a useful assay for characterization of Xist functions, including the ability to delay replication timing and induce gene silencing on autosomes (reviewed Minks and Brown, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

source: Thus, our observation that the ~7 kb RBPD RNA induces DRT/DMC on the inactive X chromosome, and associates with the Xist RNA cloud (Figure 4A and B), suggests that the ~7 kb RBPD RNA interferes with Xist RNA function within the heteromeric condensate.

claim: The ~7 kb RBPD RNA associates with the Xist RNA cloud.
source: Thus, our observation that the ~7 kb RBPD RNA induces DRT/DMC on the inactive X chromosome, and associates with the Xist RNA cloud (Figure 4A and B), suggests that the ~7 kb RBPD RNA interferes with Xist RNA function within the heteromeric condensate.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and shown in Figure 4A and B.

claim: The ~7 kb RBPD RNA interferes with Xist RNA function within the heteromeric condensate.
source: Thus, our observation that the ~7 kb RBPD RNA induces DRT/DMC on the inactive X chromosome, and associates with the Xist RNA cloud (Figure 4A and B), suggests that the ~7 kb RBPD RNA interferes with Xist RNA function within the heteromeric condensate.

source: One intriguing observation, which is largely ignored by the X inactivation field, is that deletion of the Xist gene on either the active or inactive X chromosomes results in delayed replication timing of the X chromosome (Diaz-Perez et al., 2005; Diaz-Perez et al., 2006).

source: Thus, loss of function mutations of either ASARs or Xist result in a similar chromosome-wide delayed replication timing phenotype.
